metadata.title: ARM Holdings PLC (ARM) (Q1 2027) Earnings Call Highlights: Record Revenue and AI Growth Amid ...

content.text:
This article first appeared on GuruFocus.
-
Revenue: $1.29 billion, up 22% year-over-year, a record for the first quarter.
-
Royalty Revenue: $715 million, up 22% year-over-year, a record for Q1.
-
Licensing Revenue: $574 million, up 23% year-over-year, a record for Q1.
-
Non-GAAP EPS: $0.45, up 29% year-over-year.
-
Non-GAAP Operating Margin: Approximately 41%, up 200 basis points year-over-year.
-
Non-GAAP Operating Expense: $733 million, up 18% year-over-year.
-
Free Cash Flow: $665 million in the quarter, $1.4 billion over the trailing 12 months.
-
Data Center Royalty Revenue: More than doubled year-over-year.
-
Annualized Contract Value (ACV): Grew 13% year-over-year.
-
Q2 Fiscal 2027 Guidance Revenue: Expected to be $1.38 billion, plus or minus $50 million.
-
Q2 Fiscal 2027 Guidance Non-GAAP Operating Expense: Expected to be approximately $780 million.
Release Date: July 29, 2026
For the complete transcript of the earnings call, please refer to the full earnings call transcript.
Positive Points
-
Record first-quarter revenue of $1.29 billion, up 22% year-over-year, driven by strong licensing and royalty growth.
-
Data center royalty revenue more than doubled year-over-year, driven by accelerating adoption of ARM Neoverse cores.
-
Demand for the new ARM AGI CPU now exceeds $2 billion, with increased confidence in achieving upside to the initial $1 billion opportunity.
-
Non-GAAP operating margin improved 200 basis points year-over-year to 41%, demonstrating strong operational leverage.
-
Free cash flow generation remains robust at $665 million for the quarter and $1.4 billion over the trailing twelve months.
Negative Points
-
Smartphone market weakness due to higher memory prices is impacting royalty revenue growth, with expectations lowered from ~20% to high-teens for the fiscal year.
-
Non-GAAP operating expenses increased 18% year-over-year due to ongoing R&D investments, pressuring near-term profitability.
-
The ARM AGI CPU business faces supply chain constraints across wafers, substrates, test capacity, and memory, limiting near-term revenue potential.
-
Gross margins for the initial ARM AGI CPU generation are expected to be in the high-30% to low-40% range, below the company's long-term target of 50%.
-
Licensing revenue remains lumpy due to the timing and size of high-value deals, creating quarterly volatility.
Q & A Highlights
Here are the key highlights from the ARM Holdings PLC (NASDAQ:ARM) earnings call for the first quarter of fiscal year 2027.
Q: Can you provide more detail on the increased confidence in upside to the $1 billion AGI CPU revenue opportunity?A: (Rene Haas, CEO) The confidence has increased across the board. The demand pipeline has grown from $2 billion to north of $2 billion in the last 90 days. More importantly, our ability to secure the necessary supply chain componentswafers, substrates, test capacity, and memoryhas improved significantly, giving us greater confidence in achieving more than the initial $1 billion target.
Q: How should we think about the gross margin structure for the AGI CPU business, especially with the potential for upside?A: (Jason Child, CFO) There is no change from last quarter's expectations. For the first generation, we expect gross margins in the high 30% to low 40% range for Q4 of this fiscal year and into next year. Over the next couple of years, as we bring more of the ASIC work in-house, we expect to reach 50%. We will provide a more detailed update on both revenue and margin profile at the end of Q3.
Q: Can you discuss the impact of higher memory costs on the smartphone market and your royalty revenue outlook?A: (Rene Haas, CEO & Jason Child, CFO) While the smartphone market is projected to be down, Arm is somewhat insulated due to the shift to higher-value Armv9 and CSS products, leading to double-digit royalty growth in that segment. However, the weakness is now affecting all tiers of the market, not just the low end. As a result, our full-year royalty growth expectation has shifted from ~20% to the high teens. This is being offset by continued overperformance in the cloud AI data center business.
Q: What is the demand pipeline for the AGI CPU in the out-years (FY '29-'31), and does the $15 billion projection for '31 account for supply chain headwinds?A: (Rene Haas, CEO & Jason Child, CFO) The $15 billion projection was based on our view of the supply picture at the time. The CPU TAM we discussed in March ($100 billion) may have been conservative, as peers now estimate it up to $200 billion. While supply is tight for the next couple of years, capacity is expected to expand significantly (70-100%) in calendar '28 and '29. If our market share holds, the opportunity could be much larger than the $15 billion figure.
Q: Where does the AGI CPU fit within the broader AI market, specifically in traditional servers, head nodes, and agentic applications?A: (Rene Haas, CEO) The Arm AGI CPU is a great fit for all three categories. We have customers like Cerebras and OpenAI for head node applications, and Meta and Cloudflare for agentic and general-purpose server workloads. The 128-core design is particularly efficient for running agentic workloads, where throughput is constrained by the number of CPUs.
Q: What is preventing Arm from securing supply for more than $1 billion in AGI CPU revenue, and does the rise of proprietary accelerators from partners like Nvidia, Amazon, and Google restrict Arm's opportunity?A: (Rene Haas, CEO) On supply, it is a very tight market across all components (memory, test, substrates, wafers), making even small increments difficult. However, we are more optimistic than 90 days ago. On proprietary accelerators, there is a clear space for Arm. Google uses its Arm-based Axion CPU to interface with its TPUs, and Nvidia's NVLink Fusion platform allows for mixing Arm CPUs with custom accelerators. There are clear paths for Arm to connect to custom accelerators.
Q: Are you looking at higher core counts for future AGI CPUs, and when will you start breaking out silicon revenue?A: (Rene Haas, CEO & Jason Child, CFO) On the product roadmap, the direction of travel is clearly towards more cores, as they are more efficient for agentic workloads. We have nothing specific to announce today. On revenue, we will break out silicon revenue as a separate line item once it reaches at least 10% of total revenue, which we expect in fiscal year 2028.
Q: With the incremental weakness in smartphone royalties, can licensing revenue provide upside to offset this? And is the 20% royalty growth target for FY '29 still valid?A: (Jason Child, CFO) Yes, we expect any softness in royalties to be offset by at least as much strength in licensing. For Q2, we guided to lower royalty growth (13%) but higher license growth, keeping the overall business ahead of expectations. For FY '29, the 20%+ royalty growth target is still intact. The current weakness is cyclical, and we expect a recovery in the smartphone market next year, while AI deployments continue to accelerate.
Q: Is the proliferation of low-cost AI models a net positive or negative for Arm's AGI CPU and IP business?A: (Rene Haas, CEO) It is somewhere between net neutral and net positive. Arm is agnostic to the type of AI model (open or closed source). All models require CPUs and IP to run. If open-source models lead to more efficient, smaller models that can run on edge devices, that would be a great thing for Arm given its dominant footprint in that market. Ultimately, all AI workloads need to run on Arm CPUs and IP.
Q: Can you explain the timing and cadence of R&D costs, and is there a risk of a single component shortage derailing the AGI CPU ramp?A: (Jason Child, CFO & Rene Haas, CEO) On R&D, the Q1 underspend was primarily on tools and cloud spend, not headcount. We expect to bank that savings. On the AGI CPU, there is no concern about a single point of failure. We are very confident in our supply chain partners and their capabilities, and we do not see a scenario where one missing component could tip the whole program over.
For the complete transcript of the earnings call, please refer to the full earnings call transcript.
